claim: Plant viruses represent a risk to agricultural production.
source: Plant viruses represent a risk to agricultural production and as only a few treatments exist, it is urgent to identify resistance mechanisms and factors.
evidence: This is a general statement about plant viruses in the abstract, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Only a few treatments exist for plant viruses.
source: Plant viruses represent a risk to agricultural production and as only a few treatments exist, it is urgent to identify resistance mechanisms and factors.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the limited availability of treatments for plant viral infections.

claim: Plasma membrane-localized proteins play an essential role in sensing extracellular threats presented by bacteria, fungi, or herbivores in plant immunity.
source: In plant immunity, plasma membrane (PM)-localized proteins play an essential role in sensing the extracellular threat presented by bacteria, fungi, or herbivores.
evidence: This statement represents established knowledge in plant immunity research.

claim: Viruses are intracellular pathogens.
source: Viruses are intracellular pathogens and as such the role of the plant PM in detection and resistance against viruses is often overlooked.
evidence: This is a fundamental characteristic of viruses, representing established biological knowledge.

claim: The role of the plant plasma membrane in detection and resistance against viruses is often overlooked.
source: Viruses are intracellular pathogens and as such the role of the plant PM in detection and resistance against viruses is often overlooked.
evidence: This is an inference based on the intracellular nature of viruses and the focus of plant immunity research.

claim: CPK3 displays a specific ability to hamper viral propagation over CPK isoforms that are involved in immune response to extracellular pathogens.
source: We investigated the role of the partially PM-bound Calcium-dependent protein kinase 3 (CPK3) in viral infection and we discovered that it displayed a specific ability to hamper viral propagation over CPK isoforms that are involved in immune response to extracellular pathogens.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript comparing different CPK mutants.

claim: The lateral organization of plasma membrane proteins and lipids underlies signal transduction in plants.
source: More and more evidence supports that the lateral organization of PM proteins and lipids underlies signal transduction in plants.
evidence: This statement references accumulating evidence in the field, representing emerging knowledge.

claim: CPK3 diffusion in the plasma membrane is reduced upon activation.
source: We showed here that CPK3 diffusion in the PM is reduced upon activation as well as upon viral infection and that such immobilization depended on its substrate, Remorin (REM1.2), a scaffold protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CPK3 diffusion in the plasma membrane is reduced upon viral infection.
source: We showed here that CPK3 diffusion in the PM is reduced upon activation as well as upon viral infection and that such immobilization depended on its substrate, Remorin (REM1.2), a scaffold protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM experimental data comparing mock and PlAMV-infected conditions.

claim: CPK3 immobilization upon viral infection depends on its substrate REM1.2.
source: We showed here that CPK3 diffusion in the PM is reduced upon activation as well as upon viral infection and that such immobilization depended on its substrate, Remorin (REM1.2), a scaffold protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing CPK3 dynamics in REM mutant backgrounds.

claim: REM1.2 is a scaffold protein.
source: We showed here that CPK3 diffusion in the PM is reduced upon activation as well as upon viral infection and that such immobilization depended on its substrate, Remorin (REM1.2), a scaffold protein.
evidence: This characterization of REM1.2 is based on established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Viral infection induces a CPK3-dependent increase of REM1.2 plasma membrane diffusion.
source: Furthermore, we discovered that the viral infection induced a CPK3-dependent increase of REM1.2 PM diffusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data showing REM1.2 dynamics in wild-type and cpk3 mutant backgrounds upon viral infection.

claim: The interdependence between CPK3 and REM1.2 is observable regarding viral propagation.
source: Such interdependence was also observable regarding viral propagation.
evidence: This claim is supported by viral propagation assays in various mutant backgrounds.

claim: This study unveils a complex relationship between a kinase and its substrate that contrasts with the commonly described co-stabilisation upon activation.
source: This study unveils a complex relationship between a kinase and its substrate that contrasts with the commonly described co-stabilisation upon activation while it proposes a PM-based mechanism involved in decreased sensitivity to viral infection in plants.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the experimental data showing opposite dynamics of CPK3 and REM1.2 upon viral infection.

claim: This study proposes a plasma membrane-based mechanism involved in decreased sensitivity to viral infection in plants.
source: This study unveils a complex relationship between a kinase and its substrate that contrasts with the commonly described co-stabilisation upon activation while it proposes a PM-based mechanism involved in decreased sensitivity to viral infection in plants.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Potexvirus epidemics like the one caused by pepino mosaic virus dramatically affect crop production.
source: In particular, potexvirus epidemics like the one caused by pepino mosaic virus dramatically affect crop production (Hanssen and Thomma, 2010) and the lack of chemical treatments available makes it crucial to develop inventive protective methods.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hanssen and Thomma, 2010.

claim: The lack of chemical treatments available for potexviruses makes it crucial to develop inventive protective methods.
source: In particular, potexvirus epidemics like the one caused by pepino mosaic virus dramatically affect crop production (Hanssen and Thomma, 2010) and the lack of chemical treatments available makes it crucial to develop inventive protective methods.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of treatments and the impact of viral epidemics.

claim: Plant viruses rely on mechanical wounding or insect vectors to cross the plant cell wall.
source: Unlike their animal counterparts, which enter host cells by interacting directly with the plasma membrane (PM), plant viruses have to rely either on mechanical wounding or insect vectors to cross the plant cell wall (Hanssen and Thomma, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Hanssen and Thomma, 2010, and represents established knowledge.

claim: Only a few plasma membrane-localized proteins were identified as taking part in immunity against viruses.
source: For this reason, only a few PM-localized proteins were identified as taking part in immunity against viruses (Zorzatto et al., 2015; Ngou et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations and represents the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Members of the REMORIN protein family are involved in viral propagation.
source: Among them, members of the REMORIN (REM) protein family were shown to be involved in viral propagation, with varying mechanisms depending on the studied viral genera (Cheng et al., 2020; Fu et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2022a; Raffaele et al., 2009; Rocher et al., 2022; Son et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: REMORIN proteins display varying mechanisms in viral propagation depending on the studied viral genera.
source: Among them, members of the REMORIN (REM) protein family were shown to be involved in viral propagation, with varying mechanisms depending on the studied viral genera (Cheng et al., 2020; Fu et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2022a; Raffaele et al., 2009; Rocher et al., 2022; Son et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations indicating different mechanisms across studies.

claim: REM proteins form nanodomains at the plasma membrane.
source: REM proteins are well-known for their heterogeneous distribution at the PM, forming nanodomains (ND), PM nanoscale environments that display a composition different from the surrounding PM (Gronnier et al., 2018; Jaillais and Ott, 2020, Jarsch et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Nanodomains are plasma membrane nanoscale environments that display a composition different from the surrounding plasma membrane.
source: REM proteins are well-known for their heterogeneous distribution at the PM, forming nanodomains (ND), PM nanoscale environments that display a composition different from the surrounding PM (Gronnier et al., 2018; Jaillais and Ott, 2020, Jarsch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Nanodomains play a role in signal transduction.
source: Increasing evidence supports the role of ND in signal transduction, with the underlying idea that the local accumulation of proteins allows amplification and specification of the signal (Jaillais and Ott, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents emerging knowledge in the field.

claim: Local accumulation of proteins in nanodomains allows amplification and specification of the signal.
source: Increasing evidence supports the role of ND in signal transduction, with the underlying idea that the local accumulation of proteins allows amplification and specification of the signal (Jaillais and Ott, 2020).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by a citation.

claim: Arabidopsis RHO-OF-PLANT 6 accumulates in distinct nanodomains upon osmotic stress.
source: For example, Arabidopsis RHO-OF-PLANT 6 accumulates in distinct ND upon osmotic stress and auxin treatment in a dose-dependent way for the latter (Platre et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Platre et al., 2019.

claim: Arabidopsis RHO-OF-PLANT 6 accumulates in distinct nanodomains upon auxin treatment in a dose-dependent way.
source: For example, Arabidopsis RHO-OF-PLANT 6 accumulates in distinct ND upon osmotic stress and auxin treatment in a dose-dependent way for the latter (Platre et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Platre et al., 2019.

claim: Arabidopsis REM1.2 forms clusters upon exposure to the bacterial effector flg22.
source: Recently, Arabidopsis REM1.2 (later named REM1.2) was demonstrated to form clusters upon exposure to the bacterial effector flg22 to support the condensation of Arabidopsis FORMIN 6 and to induce actin cytoskeleton remodeling (Ma et al., 2022b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2022b.

claim: REM1.2 clusters support the condensation of Arabidopsis FORMIN 6 upon flg22 exposure.
source: Recently, Arabidopsis REM1.2 (later named REM1.2) was demonstrated to form clusters upon exposure to the bacterial effector flg22 to support the condensation of Arabidopsis FORMIN 6 and to induce actin cytoskeleton remodeling (Ma et al., 2022b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2022b.

claim: REM1.2 induces actin cytoskeleton remodeling upon flg22 exposure.
source: Recently, Arabidopsis REM1.2 (later named REM1.2) was demonstrated to form clusters upon exposure to the bacterial effector flg22 to support the condensation of Arabidopsis FORMIN 6 and to induce actin cytoskeleton remodeling (Ma et al., 2022b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ma et al., 2022b.

claim: The canonical mechanism describes the accumulation of proteins in nanodomains upon stimulation.
source: However, unlike the canonical mechanism describing the accumulation of proteins in ND upon stimulation (Platre et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2022b; Smokvarska et al., 2020), we showed previously that Solanum tuberosum REM1.3 (StREM1.3) ND were disrupted and the diffusion of individual proteins increased in response to a viral infection (Perraki et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations describing the typical behavior of proteins in nanodomains.

claim: Solanum tuberosum REM1.3 nanodomains were disrupted in response to viral infection.
source: However, unlike the canonical mechanism describing the accumulation of proteins in ND upon stimulation (Platre et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2022b; Smokvarska et al., 2020), we showed previously that Solanum tuberosum REM1.3 (StREM1.3) ND were disrupted and the diffusion of individual proteins increased in response to a viral infection (Perraki et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors (Perraki et al., 2018).

claim: The diffusion of StREM1.3 individual proteins increased in response to viral infection.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors (Perraki et al., 2018).

claim: StREM1.3 lateral organization in lipid bilayers is modified upon its phosphorylation status in vitro.
source: StREM1.3 lateral organization in lipid bilayers was also shown to be modified upon its phosphorylation status, both in vitro and in vivo (Perraki et al., 2018; Legrand et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perraki et al., 2018 and Legrand et al., 2023.

claim: StREM1.3 lateral organization in lipid bilayers is modified upon its phosphorylation status in vivo.
source: StREM1.3 lateral organization in lipid bilayers was also shown to be modified upon its phosphorylation status, both in vitro and in vivo (Perraki et al., 2018; Legrand et al., 2023).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perraki et al., 2018 and Legrand et al., 2023.

claim: The role of protein dispersion upon stimuli is not understood yet.
source: The role of such protein dispersion upon stimuli is not understood yet and only a few similar cases are reported in the literature (Martinière et al., 2019; Gournas et al., 2018)
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current understanding, supported by limited citations.

claim: Only a few similar cases of protein dispersion upon stimuli are reported in the literature.
source: The role of such protein dispersion upon stimuli is not understood yet and only a few similar cases are reported in the literature (Martinière et al., 2019; Gournas et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Martinière et al., 2019 and Gournas et al., 2018.

claim: REM1.2 was identified as a substrate of CPK3.
source: REM1.2 was identified as a substrate of the partially membrane-bound calcium-dependent protein kinase 3 (CPK3) (Mehlmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mehlmer et al., 2010.

claim: CPK3 is partially membrane-bound.
source: REM1.2 was identified as a substrate of the partially membrane-bound calcium-dependent protein kinase 3 (CPK3) (Mehlmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This characterization is supported by a citation to Mehlmer et al., 2010.

claim: CPK3 is involved in defense response against herbivores.
source: CPK3 is involved in defense response against herbivores, bacteria, and viruses and was recently proposed to be at cross-roads between pattern-triggered immunity and effector-triggered immunity (Perraki et al., 2018; Kanchiswamy et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: CPK3 is involved in defense response against bacteria.
source: CPK3 is involved in defense response against herbivores, bacteria, and viruses and was recently proposed to be at cross-roads between pattern-triggered immunity and effector-triggered immunity (Perraki et al., 2018; Kanchiswamy et al., 2010; Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: CPK3 is involved in defense response against viruses.

claim: CPK3 was recently proposed to be at cross-roads between pattern-triggered immunity and effector-triggered immunity.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Transient over-expression of CPK3 in N. benthamiana hampers potato virus X cell-to-cell propagation.
source: We showed previously that transient over-expression of CPK3 in N. benthamiana was able to hamper potato virus X (PVX, potexvirus) cell-to-cell propagation (Perraki et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors (Perraki et al., 2018).

claim: The role of CPK3 plasma membrane localization in immunity was never investigated for any pathogen.
source: Although partially PM localized, the role of CPK3 PM localization in immunity was never investigated for any pathogen.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature based on the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: PVX cannot infect Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: As the PVX cannot infect Arabidopsis thaliana, the dedicated plant model for genetic studies, we used an alternative virus model able to infect this species, the plantago asiatica mosaic virus (PlAMV) (Minato et al., 2014; Yamaji et al., 2012) to investigate the role of CPK3 and of its PM localization in potexvirus propagation.
evidence: This is a known limitation of the PVX-Arabidopsis system, representing established knowledge.

claim: PlAMV can infect Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: As the PVX cannot infect Arabidopsis thaliana, the dedicated plant model for genetic studies, we used an alternative virus model able to infect this species, the plantago asiatica mosaic virus (PlAMV) (Minato et al., 2014; Yamaji et al., 2012) to investigate the role of CPK3 and of its PM localization in potexvirus propagation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Minato et al., 2014 and Yamaji et al., 2012.

claim: CPK3 plays a specific role among other immune-related CPKs in limiting PlAMV infection.
source: We were able to highlight the specific role of CPK3 among other immune-related CPKs Boudsocq et al., 2010; Gao et al., 2013; Guzel Deger et al., 2015 in this context.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different CPK mutants in viral propagation assays.

claim: CPK3 membrane localization is required to hamper viral cell-to-cell propagation.
source: Also, we demonstrated that CPK3 membrane localization was required to hamper viral cell-to-cell propagation, and using single-particle tracking photoactivated light microscopy (spt-PALM), we discovered that CPK3 diffusion was reduced upon activation and viral infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that CPK3G2A (lacking membrane anchor) does not complement the cpk3 mutant phenotype.

claim: CPK3 diffusion is reduced upon activation.
source: Also, we demonstrated that CPK3 membrane localization was required to hamper viral cell-to-cell propagation, and using single-particle tracking photoactivated light microscopy (spt-PALM), we discovered that CPK3 diffusion was reduced upon activation and viral infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data comparing CPK3 and CPK3CA (constitutively active).

claim: PlAMV-induced CPK3 plasma membrane confinement depends on the expression of Group 1 REM.
source: Interestingly, this reduction of PM diffusion depended on the expression of Group 1 REM while viral-induced REM1.2 increased PM diffusion depended on CPK3.
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data showing CPK3 dynamics in REM mutant backgrounds.

claim: Viral-induced REM1.2 increased plasma membrane diffusion depends on CPK3.
source: Interestingly, this reduction of PM diffusion depended on the expression of Group 1 REM while viral-induced REM1.2 increased PM diffusion depended on CPK3.
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data showing REM1.2 dynamics in cpk3 mutant background.

claim: No significant difference in PlAMV-GFP infection foci area was detected between Col-0, cpk1 cpk2, cpk5 cpk6, cpk1 cpk2 cpk5 cpk6 and cpk5 cpk6 cpk11.
source: No significant difference of PlAMV-GFP infection foci area was detected between Col-0, cpk1 cpk2, cpk5 cpk6, cpk1 cpk2 cpk5 cpk6 and cpk5 cpk6 cpk11, demonstrating that CPK1, CPK2, CPK5, CPK6 and CPK11 are not involved in PlAMV propagation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: CPK1, CPK2, CPK5, CPK6 and CPK11 are not involved in PlAMV propagation.
source: No significant difference of PlAMV-GFP infection foci area was detected between Col-0, cpk1 cpk2, cpk5 cpk6, cpk1 cpk2 cpk5 cpk6 and cpk5 cpk6 cpk11, demonstrating that CPK1, CPK2, CPK5, CPK6 and CPK11 are not involved in PlAMV propagation (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of phenotype in the mutants shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: A 20% increase of PlAMV-GFP infected area was observed in cpk3 cpk5 cpk6 cpk11 quadruple mutant relative to Col-0.
source: However, a 20% increase of PlAMV-GFP infected area was observed in cpk3 cpk5 cpk6 cpk11 quadruple mutant relative to the control Col-0, which indicates that CPK3 could play a specific role in viral propagation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: CPK3 plays a specific role in viral propagation.
source: However, a 20% increase of PlAMV-GFP infected area was observed in cpk3 cpk5 cpk6 cpk11 quadruple mutant relative to the control Col-0, which indicates that CPK3 could play a specific role in viral propagation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased infection in the cpk3-containing mutant shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: CPK1, 2, and 3 display the strongest kinase activity on REM1.2 in vitro.
source: CPK1, 2, and 3 displayed the strongest kinase activity on REM1.2 while CPK5, CPK6, and CPK11 displayed a residual activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CPK5, CPK6, and CPK11 display residual kinase activity on REM1.2 in vitro.
source: CPK1, 2, and 3 displayed the strongest kinase activity on REM1.2 while CPK5, CPK6, and CPK11 displayed a residual activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: All six CPKs phosphorylated the generic substrate histone.
source: In contrast, all six CPKs phosphorylated the generic substrate histone, suggesting some substrate specificity for REM1.2 in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is substrate specificity for REM1.2 among CPKs in vitro.
source: In contrast, all six CPKs phosphorylated the generic substrate histone, suggesting some substrate specificity for REM1.2 in vitro.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential phosphorylation of REM1.2 versus histone shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: CPK1 is mainly localized within the peroxisome.
source: Since CPK1 and CPK2 were described to be mainly localized within the peroxisome (Dammann et al., 2003) and endoplasmic reticulum (Lu and Hrabak, 2002), respectively, we hypothesize that they likely do not interact in vivo with PM-localized REM1.2 (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dammann et al., 2003.

claim: CPK2 is mainly localized within the endoplasmic reticulum.
source: Since CPK1 and CPK2 were described to be mainly localized within the peroxisome (Dammann et al., 2003) and endoplasmic reticulum (Lu and Hrabak, 2002), respectively, we hypothesize that they likely do not interact in vivo with PM-localized REM1.2 (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu and Hrabak, 2002.

claim: CPK1 and CPK2 likely do not interact in vivo with plasma membrane-localized REM1.2.
source: Since CPK1 and CPK2 were described to be mainly localized within the peroxisome (Dammann et al., 2003) and endoplasmic reticulum (Lu and Hrabak, 2002), respectively, we hypothesize that they likely do not interact in vivo with PM-localized REM1.2 (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the different subcellular localizations of the proteins.

claim: REM1.2 is localized at the plasma membrane.
source: Since CPK1 and CPK2 were described to be mainly localized within the peroxisome (Dammann et al., 2003) and endoplasmic reticulum (Lu and Hrabak, 2002), respectively, we hypothesize that they likely do not interact in vivo with PM-localized REM1.2 (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huang et al., 2019.

claim: In both cpk3-1 and cpk3-2 KO lines, PlAMV-GFP propagation was significantly enhanced (40 to 60% compared with WT Col-0).
source: In both cpk3-1 and cpk3-2 KO lines, PlAMV-GFP propagation was significantly enhanced (40 to 60% compared with WT Col-0), whereas the over-expression lines Pro35S:CPK3-HA-OE#8.2 and Pro35S:CPK3-HA-OE#16.272 showed 10% and 20% restriction of the foci area, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pro35S:CPK3-HA-OE#8.2 showed 10% restriction of PlAMV-GFP foci area.
source: In both cpk3-1 and cpk3-2 KO lines, PlAMV-GFP propagation was significantly enhanced (40 to 60% compared with WT Col-0), whereas the over-expression lines Pro35S:CPK3-HA-OE#8.2 and Pro35S:CPK3-HA-OE#16.272 showed 10% and 20% restriction of the foci area, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pro35S:CPK3-HA-OE#16.2 showed 20% restriction of PlAMV-GFP foci area.
source: In both cpk3-1 and cpk3-2 KO lines, PlAMV-GFP propagation was significantly enhanced (40 to 60% compared with WT Col-0), whereas the over-expression lines Pro35S:CPK3-HA-OE#8.2 and Pro35S:CPK3-HA-OE#16.272 showed 10% and 20% restriction of the foci area, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Loss of CPK3 leads to an increase of PlAMV-GFP propagation in distal leaves.
source: We observed that loss of CPK3 led to an increase of PlAMV-GFP propagation in distal leaves during the course of our assay while the overexpression of CPK3 did not hamper PlAMV-GFP to a greater extent than WT Col-0 (Figure 1D and E).

claim: Overexpression of CPK3 did not hamper PlAMV-GFP systemic propagation to a greater extent than WT Col-0.
source: We observed that loss of CPK3 led to an increase of PlAMV-GFP propagation in distal leaves during the course of our assay while the overexpression of CPK3 did not hamper PlAMV-GFP to a greater extent than WT Col-0 (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: CPK3 effect on PlAMV propagation is predominant at the site of infection.
source: This would suggest that CPK3 effect on PlAMV propagation is predominant at the site of infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects observed in local versus systemic infection assays.

claim: CPK3 Lysine 107 functions as an ATP binding site.
source: CPK3 Lysine 107 functions as an ATP binding site and its substitution into methionine abolishes CPK3 activity in vitro (Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lu et al., 2020.

claim: Substitution of CPK3 Lysine 107 into methionine abolishes CPK3 activity in vitro.
source: CPK3 Lysine 107 functions as an ATP binding site and its substitution into methionine abolishes CPK3 activity in vitro (Lu et al., 2020).

claim: CPK3K107M can no longer phosphorylate REM1.2 in vitro.
source: In good agreement, we observed that CPK3K107M can no longer phosphorylate REM1.2 in vitro (Figure 1F).

claim: WT CPK3 fully complemented cpk3-2 mutant in PlAMV infection assays.

claim: cpk3-2/Pro35S:CPK3K107M displayed larger infection foci area compared to WT Col-0.

claim: CPK3 kinase activity is required for its function during PlAMV infection.
source: While the WT CPK3 fully complemented cpk3-2 mutant, it was not the case with cpk3-2/Pro35S:CPK3K107M, which displayed larger infection foci area compared to WT Col-0 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure of the kinase-dead mutant to complement the cpk3-2 phenotype shown in Figure 1G.

claim: CPK3 transcript levels remain unchanged during PlAMV infection.
source: RT-qPCR and western blots of CPK3 in Col-0 showed that both transcript and protein levels remained unchanged during PlAMV infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CPK3 protein levels remain unchanged during PlAMV infection.
source: RT-qPCR and western blots of CPK3 in Col-0 showed that both transcript and protein levels remained unchanged during PlAMV infection (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CPK3 is myristoylated at Glycine 2.
source: CPK3 is partially localized within the PM and is myristoylated at Glycine 2, a modification required for its association with membranes (Mehlmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mehlmer et al., 2010.

claim: Myristoylation at Glycine 2 is required for CPK3 association with membranes.
source: CPK3 is partially localized within the PM and is myristoylated at Glycine 2, a modification required for its association with membranes (Mehlmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mehlmer et al., 2010.

claim: ProUbi10:CPK3G2A-mRFP1.2 did not complement cpk3-2 in PlAMV infection assays.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CPK3 association with the plasma membrane is required for its function in inhibiting PlAMV propagation.
source: These observations indicate that CPK3 association with the PM is required for its function in inhibiting PlAMV propagation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure of CPK3G2A to complement the cpk3-2 phenotype shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CPK3 displays a heterogeneous pattern at the plasma membrane in both mock and PlAMV-infected conditions.
source: Imaging of the surface of A. thaliana leaf epidermal cells expressing CPK3-mRFP1.2 showed that the protein displayed a heterogeneous pattern at the PM in both conditions (Figure 2C), although the limitation in lateral resolution of confocal microscopy hindered a more detailed analysis of CPK3 PM organization.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CPK3 diffusion coefficient is reduced upon PlAMV infection.
source: We observed that CPK3 proteins were overall mobile in control and infected conditions (log(D) > –2; Figure 2E) although CPK3 diffusion was reduced upon PlAMV infection (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: CPK3 proteins are overall mobile in control and infected conditions.
source: We observed that CPK3 proteins were overall mobile in control and infected conditions (log(D) > –2; Figure 2E) although CPK3 diffusion was reduced upon PlAMV infection (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CPK3 displays a more confined behavior during PlAMV infection than in healthy conditions.
source: Analysis of the mean squared displacement (MSD), describing the surface explored by single molecules overtime, showed that CPK3 displayed a more confined behavior during a PlAMV infection than in healthy conditions (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: No difference occurs in CPK3 cluster size upon viral infection.
source: Voronoï analysis showed that no difference occurred in CPK3 cluster size or proportion of protein localized in cluster upon viral infection (Figure 2H–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by Voronoï tessellation analysis shown in Figure 2H-K.

claim: No difference occurs in the proportion of CPK3 localized in clusters upon viral infection.
source: Voronoï analysis showed that no difference occurred in CPK3 cluster size or proportion of protein localized in cluster upon viral infection (Figure 2H–K).
evidence: This claim is supported by Voronoï tessellation analysis shown in Figure 2H-K.

claim: CPK3 diffusion parameters are modified upon PlAMV infection while the nano-organization of the proteins is maintained.
source: Taken together, these results show that CPK3 diffusion parameters were modified upon PlAMV infection, although the nano-organization of the proteins was maintained.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the spt-PALM and Voronoï analysis data.

claim: CPK3 bears an auto-inhibitory domain that folds over the kinase domain and inhibits its kinase activity in the absence of calcium.
source: CPK3 bears an auto-inhibitory domain that folds over the kinase domain and inhibits its kinase activity in the absence of calcium (Sheen, 1996; Harper et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sheen, 1996 and Harper et al., 2004.

claim: Truncation of CPK3 auto-inhibitory domain along with the C-terminal regulatory domain results in a calcium-independent, constitutively active CPK3.
source: The truncation of this domain along with the C-terminal regulatory domain results in a calcium-independent, constitutively active CPK3 (CPK3CA) (Boudsocq et al., 2010) that is lethal when stably expressed in Arabidopsis (Huimin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Boudsocq et al., 2010 and Huimin et al., 2021.

claim: CPK3CA is lethal when stably expressed in Arabidopsis.
source: The truncation of this domain along with the C-terminal regulatory domain results in a calcium-independent, constitutively active CPK3 (CPK3CA) (Boudsocq et al., 2010) that is lethal when stably expressed in Arabidopsis (Huimin et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Huimin et al., 2021.

claim: ProUbi10:CPK3CA-mRFP1.2 displays a plasma membrane organization in domains discernable by confocal microscopy.
source: We observed that although both ProUbi10:CPK3-mRFP1.2 and ProUbi10:CPK3CA-mRFP1.2 were partially cytosolic when transiently expressed in N. benthamiana (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), ProUbi10:CPK3CA-mRFP1.2 displayed a PM organization in domains discernable by confocal microscopy (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The fraction of immobile CPK3CA-mEOS3.2 molecules is more abundant than for CPK3-mEOS3.2 in absence of viral infection.
source: We observed that the fraction of immobile ProUbi10:CPK3CA-mEOS3.2 molecules (log(D) < –2) is more abundant than for ProUbi10:CPK3-mEOS3.2 in absence of viral infection while no significant difference could be deciphered upon PlAMV infection (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: No significant difference in the fraction of immobile molecules could be deciphered between CPK3 and CPK3CA upon PlAMV infection.
source: We observed that the fraction of immobile ProUbi10:CPK3CA-mEOS3.2 molecules (log(D) < –2) is more abundant than for ProUbi10:CPK3-mEOS3.2 in absence of viral infection while no significant difference could be deciphered upon PlAMV infection (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: The motion of CPK3-mEOS3.2 mobile fraction is less confined than the one of CPK3CA-mEOS3.2.
source: In addition, MSD analysis showed that the motion of CPK3-mEOS3.2 mobile fraction is less confined than the one of CPK3CA-mEOS3.2 and CPK3-mEOS3.2 upon PlAMV infection (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The mobile fraction of CPK3 is affected upon PlAMV infection.
source: Overall, this indicates that the mobile and immobile fraction of CPK3 is affected upon PlAMV infection and upon truncation of its auto-inhibitory domain, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the MSD and diffusion coefficient data.

claim: The immobile fraction of CPK3 is affected upon truncation of its auto-inhibitory domain.
source: Overall, this indicates that the mobile and immobile fraction of CPK3 is affected upon PlAMV infection and upon truncation of its auto-inhibitory domain, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of CPK3 and CPK3CA diffusion data.

claim: No significant differences in distribution of cluster sizes were observed between CPK3, CPK3+PlAMV, and CPK3CA.
source: Although we did not observe any significant differences in distribution of cluster sizes between all compared conditions (Figure 3G and H), CPK3CA displayed a significantly higher proportion of proteins localized in ND compared to CPK3 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Voronoï tessellation analysis shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: CPK3CA displays a significantly higher proportion of proteins localized in nanodomains compared to CPK3.
source: Although we did not observe any significant differences in distribution of cluster sizes between all compared conditions (Figure 3G and H), CPK3CA displayed a significantly higher proportion of proteins localized in ND compared to CPK3 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Voronoï tessellation analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Treatment with fenpropimorph abolishes CPK3CA nanodomain organization.
source: We observed that the integrity of ProUbi10:CPK3CA-mRFP1.2 organization relied on sterols and phosphoinositides. Indeed, treatment with fenpropimorph, a well-described inhibitor of sterol biosynthesis (He et al., 2003), abolished CPK3CA ND organization (Figure 3J), and the co-expression of ProUbi10:CPK3CA-mRFP1.2 with the yeast phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P)-specific phosphatase SAC1 targeted to the PM (Simon et al., 2016), led to sparser and bigger domains (Figure 3K), which suggested that PI4P is not required for CPK3CA ND formation but for its regulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Fenpropimorph is a well-described inhibitor of sterol biosynthesis.
source: Indeed, treatment with fenpropimorph, a well-described inhibitor of sterol biosynthesis (He et al., 2003), abolished CPK3CA ND organization (Figure 3J)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to He et al., 2003.

claim: Co-expression of CPK3CA with PM-targeted SAC1 leads to sparser and bigger domains.
source: the co-expression of ProUbi10:CPK3CA-mRFP1.2 with the yeast phosphatidylinositol-4-phosphate (PI4P)-specific phosphatase SAC1 targeted to the PM (Simon et al., 2016), led to sparser and bigger domains (Figure 3K)
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: PI4P is not required for CPK3CA nanodomain formation but for its regulation.
source: which suggested that PI4P is not required for CPK3CA ND formation but for its regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of SAC1 on CPK3CA domain organization shown in Figure 3K.

claim: The integrity of CPK3CA organization relies on sterols and phosphoinositides.
source: We observed that the integrity of ProUbi10:CPK3CA-mRFP1.2 organization relied on sterols and phosphoinositides.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of fenpropimorph and SAC1 on CPK3CA organization.

claim: Either removal of the auto-inhibitory domain or infection with PlAMV-GFP modifies CPK3 dynamics within the plasma membrane.
source: All together these observations show that either removal of the auto-inhibitory domain or infection with PlAMV-GFP modifies CPK3 dynamics within the PM; a mechanism which could be at stake for kinase activation.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the collective spt-PALM data.

claim: Modification of CPK3 dynamics could be a mechanism for kinase activation.
source: All together these observations show that either removal of the auto-inhibitory domain or infection with PlAMV-GFP modifies CPK3 dynamics within the PM; a mechanism which could be at stake for kinase activation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observed changes in CPK3 dynamics.

claim: Group 1 REMs are substrates of CPK3.
source: Group 1 REMs are one of the targets of CPK3 and we previously demonstrated that the restriction of PVX propagation by CPK3 overexpression depended on endogenous group 1 NbREMs (Perraki et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The restriction of PVX propagation by CPK3 overexpression depends on endogenous group 1 NbREMs.
source: Group 1 REMs are one of the targets of CPK3 and we previously demonstrated that the restriction of PVX propagation by CPK3 overexpression depended on endogenous group 1 NbREMs (Perraki et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perraki et al., 2018.

claim: Four REM isoforms belong to group 1 in Arabidopsis: REM1.1, REM1.2, REM1.3, and REM1.4.
source: Four REM isoforms belong to the group 1 in Arabidopsis: REM1.1, REM1.2, REM1.3, and REM1.4 (Raffaele et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Raffaele et al., 2007.

claim: REM1.2 and REM1.3 are amongst the 10% most abundant transcripts in Arabidopsis leaves.
source: REM1.2 and REM1.3 are amongst the 10% most abundant transcripts in Arabidopsis leaves while REM1.1 was not detected in recently published leaf transcriptomes and proteomes (Mergner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mergner et al., 2020.

claim: REM1.1 was not detected in recently published leaf transcriptomes and proteomes.
source: REM1.2 and REM1.3 are amongst the 10% most abundant transcripts in Arabidopsis leaves while REM1.1 was not detected in recently published leaf transcriptomes and proteomes (Mergner et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mergner et al., 2020.

claim: REMs are scaffold proteins.
source: REMs are described as scaffold proteins (Lefebvre et al., 2010), for which physiological function depends on the proteins they interact with and their phosphorylation status (Gouguet et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lefebvre et al., 2010 and Gouguet et al., 2021.

claim: REM physiological function depends on the proteins they interact with and their phosphorylation status.
source: REMs are described as scaffold proteins (Lefebvre et al., 2010), for which physiological function depends on the proteins they interact with and their phosphorylation status (Gouguet et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gouguet et al., 2021.

claim: REM1.2 and REM1.3 share 95% of their interactome.
source: As recently described in Abel et al., 2021, REM1.2 and REM1.3 share 95% of their interactome, suggesting that they are functionally redundant.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Abel et al., 2021.

claim: REM1.2 and REM1.3 are functionally redundant.
source: As recently described in Abel et al., 2021, REM1.2 and REM1.3 share 95% of their interactome, suggesting that they are functionally redundant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the shared interactome data cited from Abel et al., 2021.

claim: No difference in PlAMV-GFP propagation was observed in rem1.2, rem1.3, or rem1.4 single mutants compared to Col-0.
source: No difference in PlAMV-GFP propagation could be observed in the single mutants, compared to Col-0 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The double mutant rem1.2 rem1.3 shows a significant increase of infection foci area compared to Col-0.
source: However, the double mutant rem1.2 rem1.3 showed a significant increase of infection foci area compared to Col-0, which was further enhanced in rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 triple KO mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The infection foci area increase in rem1.2 rem1.3 was further enhanced in rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 triple KO mutant.
source: However, the double mutant rem1.2 rem1.3 showed a significant increase of infection foci area compared to Col-0, which was further enhanced in rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 triple KO mutant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: REM1.2, REM1.3, and REM1.4 are functionally redundant regarding PlAMV cell-to-cell propagation.
source: Such additive effect of multiple mutations shows that REM1.2, REM1.3, and REM1.4 are functionally redundant regarding PlAMV cell-to-cell propagation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the additive effects observed in the mutant combinations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 displays an increased infection surface of systemic leaves compared to Col-0.
source: Finally, PlAMV-GFP systemic propagation was followed in whole plants every 3–4 d from 10 to 17 dpi, and rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 displayed an increased infection surface of systemic leaves compared to Col-0 (Figure 4B and C), suggesting that group 1 REMs are involved in both local and systemic propagation of PlAMV-GFP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: Group 1 REMs are involved in both local and systemic propagation of PlAMV-GFP.
source: Finally, PlAMV-GFP systemic propagation was followed in whole plants every 3–4 d from 10 to 17 dpi, and rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 displayed an increased infection surface of systemic leaves compared to Col-0 (Figure 4B and C), suggesting that group 1 REMs are involved in both local and systemic propagation of PlAMV-GFP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased infection in both local and systemic assays shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Neither REM1.2, REM1.3, nor REM1.4 transcript levels are modified upon PlAMV infection.
source: RT-qPCR and western blots showed that neither transcripts nor protein levels were modified upon PlAMV infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: REM protein levels are not modified upon PlAMV infection.
source: RT-qPCR and western blots showed that neither transcripts nor protein levels were modified upon PlAMV infection (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of REM1.2 is significantly increased upon PlAMV infection.
source: The diffusion coefficient of ProUbi10:mEOS3.2-REM1.2 was significantly increased upon PlAMV infection (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: REM1.2 mean squared displacement is increased upon PlAMV infection to a similar extent as StREM1.3 during PVX infection.
source: Moreover, its MSD was increased to a similar extent as what was previously observed with StREM1.3 during a PVX infection (Perraki et al., 2018; Figure 4H), although REM1.2 is overall more mobile than StREM1.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by MSD analysis shown in Figure 4H and comparison to previous work cited.

claim: REM1.2 is overall more mobile than StREM1.3.
source: Moreover, its MSD was increased to a similar extent as what was previously observed with StREM1.3 during a PVX infection (Perraki et al., 2018; Figure 4H), although REM1.2 is overall more mobile than StREM1.3.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the MSD data and previous work.

claim: REM1.2 nanodomain organization does not show any difference upon PlAMV infection.
source: Tessellation analysis of protein localization did not show any difference in ND organization, whether in size or regarding the enrichment of proteins in ND (Figure 4I–L).
evidence: This claim is supported by Voronoï tessellation analysis shown in Figure 4I-L.

claim: PlAMV infection promotes an increased diffusion of REM1.2 in the same way as PVX did with StREM1.3.
source: PlAMV infection promoted an increased diffusion of REM1.2, in the same way as PVX did with StREM1.3.
evidence: This is a comparison based on the current data and previous work on StREM1.3.

claim: The conservation of increased REM diffusion upon viral infection between plants of different families is indicative of its physiological importance.
source: The conservation of such mechanism between plants of different families is indicative of its physiological importance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conservation of the mechanism across species.

claim: Group 1 REMs from A. thaliana were previously identified as in vitro substrates of CPK3.
source: Group 1 REMs from A. thaliana were previously identified as in vitro substrates of CPK3 (Mehlmer et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mehlmer et al., 2010.

claim: CPK3 was identified as an interactor of REM1.2 in A. thaliana by untargeted immunoprecipitation experiments coupled to mass spectrometry.
source: Moreover, untargeted immunoprecipitation experiments coupled to mass spectrometry identified CPK3 as an interactor of REM1.2 in A. thaliana (Abel et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Abel et al., 2021.

claim: No significant additive effect was observed between the quadruple mutant lines rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 cpk3, cpk3-2, and rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4.
source: The analysis of PlAMV-GFP propagation showed that no significant additive effect could be observed between the quadruple mutant lines, cpk3-2 and rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Group 1 REMs and CPK3 function in the same signaling pathway to inhibit PlAMV propagation.
source: This indicates that group 1 REMs and CPK3 function in the same signaling pathway to inhibit PlAMV propagation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of additive effect in the quadruple mutant shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Both the diffusion coefficient and MSD of REM1.2 are not affected during viral infection in cpk3-2 background.
source: Strikingly, we observed that both the diffusion coefficient and MSD of REM1.2 were not anymore affected during a viral infection (Figure 5C–F), showing that REM1.2 PM lateral diffusion upon PlAMV infection depends on CPK3.
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 5C-F.

claim: REM1.2 plasma membrane lateral diffusion upon PlAMV infection depends on CPK3.
source: Strikingly, we observed that both the diffusion coefficient and MSD of REM1.2 were not anymore affected during a viral infection (Figure 5C–F), showing that REM1.2 PM lateral diffusion upon PlAMV infection depends on CPK3.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of REM1.2 diffusion changes in cpk3 mutant shown in Figure 5C-F.

claim: The diffusion coefficient and MSD of CPK3 in rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 triple KO background remain the same during infection compared to control condition.
source: Similarly, the diffusion coefficient and the MSD of mEOS3.2-CPK3 in rem1.2 rem1.3 rem1.4 triple KO background remained the same during an infection compared to control condition (Figure 5G–J), unlike what was observed in a Col-0 background (Figure 2D–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 5G-J.

claim: The confinement of CPK3 proteins upon viral infection depends on the presence of group 1 REMs.
source: This result indicated that the confinement of CPK3 proteins upon viral infection depended on the presence of group 1 REMs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of CPK3 confinement in REM mutant background shown in Figure 5G-J.

claim: Group 1 REMs play a role in CPK3 domain regulation upon viral infection.
source: This showed that group 1 REMs might play a role in CPK3 domain regulation upon viral infection.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the reduced CPK3 clustering in REM mutant upon infection shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Upon transient co-expression with CPK3CA, REM diffusion is significantly increased.
source: Upon transient co-expression with CPK3CA, REM diffusion was significantly increased.
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: CPK3CA-G2A is not able to increase REM diffusion.
source: We tested if CPK3CA-G2A was still able to hinder REM diffusion, which was not the case.
evidence: This claim is supported by spt-PALM data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: Plasma membrane-bound CPK3 plays a specific role in REM increased diffusion upon viral infection.
source: All these data support a specific role of PM-bound CPK3 in REM increased diffusion upon viral infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective data showing CPK3CA effects on REM diffusion.

claim: CPK3 and REM randomly colocalize in both mock and PlAMV-infected conditions.
source: Using confocal microscopy, we showed that they randomly colocalized in both situations (Figure 5—figure supplement 5), the interaction between the kinase and its substrate probably occurring in a narrow spatiotemporal window.
evidence: This claim is supported by colocalization analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: The interaction between CPK3 and REM1.2 probably occurs in a narrow spatiotemporal window.
source: the interaction between the kinase and its substrate probably occurring in a narrow spatiotemporal window.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the random colocalization observed.

claim: There is a strong inter-dependence of group 1 REMs and CPK3 in their physiological function upon PlAMV infection.
source: Taken all together, those results show a strong inter-dependence of group 1 REMs and CPK3 both in their physiological function and in their PM lateral diffusion upon PlAMV infection.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on the collective genetic and biophysical data.

claim: There is a strong inter-dependence of group 1 REMs and CPK3 in their plasma membrane lateral diffusion upon PlAMV infection.
